sections.heading: Your purpose is to make Jesus loved and honored
sections.text: Father, I believe your great purpose is to make your Son glorious and deeply loved. Jesus is risen and ascended, and one day all who belong to him will see his glory clearly and love him without end. My love for him now is small and mixed with so much weakness, but please make that future my own: to see him, love him, and praise him forever.
theological_themes: God's saving purpose is centered on the glory of Christ.
Christ is ascended and will be adored forever by his people.
The believer longs for fuller love for Christ than is possible in this present weakness.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus prays that those the Father has given him would be with him and see his glory. This directly supports the prayer's hope of finally beholding Christ and loving him perfectly.
Paul describes the Father's exaltation of Jesus and the universal confession of his lordship. It grounds the prayer's claim that God's purpose is the glory and honor of Christ.

sections.heading: You have begun in me what you will finish
sections.text: Even now, you have given me a real beginning. I do not see Jesus as clearly as I will one day, but you have opened my eyes enough to know him, receive him, trust him, and belong to him. Teach me to love him not only in private thoughts, but in what I say, how I live, and what I delight in.
theological_themes: God begins the believer's knowledge and love of Christ in this life and will complete it in glory.
Faith receives Christ personally, not merely as an idea.
Love for Christ should shape the heart, speech, and daily life.

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts our present partial knowledge with the clear knowledge believers will have in the age to come. This supports the prayer's tension between real present faith and future fullness.
Paul speaks of receiving Christ Jesus the Lord and continuing to walk in him. That fits the prayer's movement from receiving Christ to living a life rooted in him.

sections.heading: Let love for Christ shape my worship and obedience
sections.text: Help me give attention to the practices and patterns that keep my heart near you: worship, prayer, obedience, self-control, and the steady listening to your Word. Keep me from doing these things to impress anyone or to earn your favor. Let me do them because I love Christ, because I am grateful, and because I want to know and keep his will.
theological_themes: Christian discipline and worship are responses of love and gratitude, not attempts to earn salvation.
Obedience flows from love for Christ.
The believer must intentionally guard and cultivate a Christ-centered heart.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus connects love for him with keeping his commandments. This grounds the prayer's desire to seek and obey Christ's will from love rather than mere duty.
Paul urges believers, in view of God's mercy, to offer themselves to God in worshipful obedience. This supports the prayer's emphasis on gratitude as the motive for disciplined devotion.

sections.heading: Make Christ the center of my life and happiness
sections.text: You have been teaching me that my life and joy are found in belonging to Christ. Keep my heart and mind centered on him. Make union with him more precious to me than comfort, approval, success, or control. And make me more like him—not closed in on myself, but ready to share good with others because he has been so generous to me. If Christ is mine and I am his, that is already a taste of heaven here on earth.
theological_themes: The believer's deepest identity and joy are found in union with Christ.
Christ is sufficient as the center of the heart and mind.
Union with Christ produces Christlike generosity and love toward others.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the believer's life as crucified with Christ and now lived by faith in the Son of God. This supports the prayer's language of finding one's life in oneness with Christ.
Paul's statement that to live is Christ expresses the Christ-centered life the prayer asks for: happiness, purpose, and identity gathered into him.
Paul teaches that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works prepared by God. This connects union with Christ to the practical outflow of doing good to others.

sections.heading: Carry me by your Spirit toward the city to come
sections.text: But Father, I cannot keep walking this road by my own strength. I need the power, life, and steady prompting of your Spirit to carry me forward. Keep moving me toward the Jerusalem that is above, toward the home you have promised, when my faith will become sight and my love will be whole.
theological_themes: The Christian life depends on the ongoing work and power of the Holy Spirit.
Believers are pilgrims moving toward the heavenly city God has promised.
Present sanctification is sustained by God, not by self-reliance.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that believers put sin to death by the Spirit and are led by the Spirit as God's children. This grounds the prayer's dependence on the Spirit for perseverance and growth.
Hebrews describes believers as having come to the heavenly Jerusalem through Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant. This illuminates the prayer's image of being carried toward the true Jerusalem.

sections.heading: Let me live like Jesus until I die in peace
sections.text: While I am still in this world, let me represent Jesus faithfully. Teach me to do what he would have me do, to live in the way he has shown, and to walk with love, gentleness, and humility. Make my life the kind of life through which others can recognize him. And when death comes, let me meet it with peace because I have lived and died belonging to Christ.
theological_themes: Christians are called to imitate Christ in ordinary life.
Love, meekness, and humility make Christ visible through his people.
Peace in death rests on belonging to Christ.

scripture_references.connection: John says that whoever abides in Christ ought to walk as Jesus walked. This directly supports the prayer's desire to live in the world as Christ would have lived.
Paul calls believers to imitate God as beloved children and walk in love, following Christ's self-giving pattern. This grounds the prayer's emphasis on love and Christlike conduct.
Paul faces life and death with confidence because Christ will be honored in him and death means being with Christ. This supports the prayer's longing for peace at death through belonging to Jesus.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses the phrase “all the elect,” which reflects a Reformed theological framework. I rendered it as “all who belong to him” to preserve the idea of God's chosen people without making the modern prayer sound like a doctrinal formula.

The prayer strongly frames God's ultimate purpose as the glorification and love of Christ. This is biblically grounded, but it reflects a particular theological emphasis that may feel more explicit than some contemporary devotional language.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Discipline, and all the ways of worship” was interpreted as the ordinary practices of Christian devotion and obedience—worship, prayer, self-control, and attention to Scripture—rather than as church discipline in the corrective sense.
“My Jerusalem” was interpreted as the heavenly Jerusalem, the believer's final home with God, rather than an earthly city or a private spiritual achievement.
“To be as Christ in this world” was rendered as faithful representation and imitation of Jesus, not as becoming Christ in essence or sharing his unique mediatorial role.
